title: Does shape affect how far a substance gets into a block?

stimulus.title: Does shape affect how far a substance gets into a block?
stimulus.html: A student has a tray of agar dyed with an indicator that is pink when basic and turns clear in acid, a beaker of dilute vinegar, a knife, a ruler and a timer. She wants to find out whether the shape of a cell, not just its size, affects how much of its volume a substance can reach by diffusion in a given time. She plans to cut blocks that all have a volume of 8 cm³ but different shapes: a 2 × 2 × 2 cm cube, a 4 × 2 × 1 cm block and an 8 × 2 × 0.5 cm slab.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the null hypothesis for this investigation.

rubric.point: States that block shape (or surface area-to-volume ratio, at equal volume) has no effect on the percentage of the block's volume that turns clear in a set time.
accept: there is no difference in the percentage cleared among the three shapes
shape does not affect how much of the block the acid reaches

parts.sample: For blocks of the same volume, shape has no effect on the percentage of the block that turns clear after a set time in vinegar.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and one variable that must be held constant, and justify holding that variable constant.

rubric.point: Identifies shape (or surface area-to-volume ratio) as the independent variable AND names a variable to hold constant (soaking time, vinegar concentration or volume, temperature, block volume, agar batch) with a reason (it also affects how far acid spreads, so changing it would confound the result).
accept: IV shape; keep soaking time the same because longer soaking lets acid go deeper
IV surface area ÷ volume; same vinegar concentration because stronger acid clears more

parts.sample: The independent variable is the shape of the block (its surface area ÷ volume: 3, 3.5 and 5.25 per cm). Soaking time must be the same for every block, because a block left in longer would clear more no matter its shape.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe how the student should measure the dependent variable, and explain why she should test several blocks of each shape.

rubric.point: Describes cutting each block after soaking and measuring the clear depth (or the size of the pink core) to calculate the percentage of volume cleared, AND explains that repeated blocks let her calculate a mean and judge variation, so one unusual block does not decide the result.
accept: measure the pink core and subtract its volume from 8 cm³; replicates reduce the effect of random error
several trials per shape to find a mean and spread

parts.sample: After 10 minutes she should cut each block in half, measure the dimensions of the pink core, calculate its volume, and find the percentage of the 8 cm³ that turned clear. Testing five blocks of each shape lets her calculate a mean and see how much the results vary, so one badly cut block does not decide the outcome.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict the results if the null hypothesis is rejected, and justify your prediction in terms of surface area and distance.

rubric.point: Predicts that the flattest block (the slab) has the largest percentage cleared and the cube the smallest, because the slab has the highest surface area ÷ volume and no point far from a surface, so acid diffusing a fixed distance reaches more of it.
accept: slab clears most, cube least, because more surface per volume and shorter distance to the center
percentage cleared rises with surface area to volume ratio

parts.sample: The slab would clear the largest share and the cube the smallest. The slab has the most surface for its volume (42 cm² against 24 cm² for the cube), and its center is only 0.25 cm from a face, so acid that spreads the same distance from each face reaches almost all of it, while the cube's center, 1 cm in, stays pink.
